edges.basis: Isaiah and Mark place the Spirit on a Davidic or messianic figure. Isaiah develops just rule; Mark narrates an event without repeating that commission.

edges.basis: Mark receives Isaiah’s wilderness-way language inside a combined opening citation. Mark’s heading joins source lines that remain distinguishable in the prophets.
edges.label: The prophetic voice and Mark’s messenger

edges.basis: Divine delight and Spirit language make Isaiah 42 a material source for hearing Matthew’s voice. The Gospel wording is not a single-source verbatim quotation.

edges.basis: Luke explicitly places Isaiah 61 on Jesus’ lips after the baptism and wilderness. The Nazareth fulfillment statement develops mission beyond what Luke’s baptism scene says by itself.

edges.basis: Malachi and Matthew place a preparing messenger before arrival and judgment. Matthew distributes Malachi’s images across John’s work and the coming one’s work.

edges.basis: Both witnesses preserve repentance, fruit, warning, water, and the coming stronger one. Luke adds dated public history, vocational answers, popular Christ expectation, and the imprisonment notice.

edges.basis: Malachi promises Elijah while John says he is not Elijah. Other Gospel role-language prevents either statement from being ignored or forced into a simple identity claim.
edges.label: Elijah promised and John’s denial

edges.basis: Both preserve Jesus, John, water, opened heaven, descending Spirit, and the voice. Matthew adds John’s objection and third-person proclamation; Mark uses torn-heaven language and direct address.
edges.label: Matthew and Mark at the Jordan

edges.basis: Both preserve baptism, Spirit, dove comparison, beloved Son, and divine pleasure. Luke adds the people and prayer while omitting the baptizer’s identity in the bounded scene.
edges.label: Matthew and Luke at the Jordan

edges.basis: Mark narrates the event; John’s Gospel reports the baptizer’s sign and testimony. John’s source omits the water act while expanding recognition, remaining, Lamb, and testimony language.
edges.label: Narrated baptism and retrospective testimony

edges.basis: Successive scenes move from John’s denied identities to his positive witness about Jesus. John names what he is not before explaining how the Spirit-sign authorizes what he says about Jesus.
edges.label: John questioned and John testifying

edges.basis: John’s testimony is repeated and two disciples begin following Jesus. Recognition by the witness and response by hearers remain distinct actions.
edges.label: The sign becomes a path of following

edges.basis: Matthew moves directly from the voice to challenges beginning “If you are the Son.” Divine declaration precedes testing; the testing does not create the sonship it challenges.
edges.label: Beloved Son and tested Son

edges.basis: Mark connects Spirit descent, Spirit driving, testing, John’s arrest, and Jesus’ announcement. The same Spirit appears in descent and driving without the text treating those acts as identical.
edges.label: Torn heaven, driven wilderness, and proclamation

edges.basis: Luke carries Jesus from prayer and Spirit descent to Spirit fullness and wilderness testing. The narrative links the scenes while leaving why this testing follows the voice unexplained.
edges.label: Prayer, Spirit fullness, and testing

edges.basis: John’s earlier sign-authorized testimony develops into an explicit refusal of rivalry. The later scene adds bridegroom and above/below language beyond the baptism testimony.
edges.label: Recognition at the Jordan and decreasing prominence

edges.basis: Adjacent reports attribute baptizing to Jesus’ circle. John 4 clarifies that the disciples perform the physical action even when the work is associated with Jesus.
edges.label: Reported baptizing and the narrator’s clarification

edges.basis: Both preserve the coming-one question and Jesus’ appeal to observed deeds. Luke places deeds in the immediate hour and explicitly names responses to John’s baptism.
edges.label: John’s prison question in Matthew and Luke

edges.basis: Both narrate marriage confrontation, imprisonment, banquet oath, beheading, burial, and report. Mark expands Herod’s fear, protection, perplexity, and repeated listening.
edges.label: John’s death in Matthew and Mark

edges.basis: Both witnesses preserve Jesus’ counterquestion and the leaders’ calculation. Matthew extends the exchange with the two sons and unbelief after seeing others respond.
edges.label: John’s baptism in two authority disputes

edges.basis: Both preserve heaven/human alternatives, fear of the people, and professed ignorance. Luke locates the exchange while Jesus teaches and announces good news in the Temple.
edges.label: The authority deadlock in Mark and Luke

edges.basis: Matthew and Acts place baptism language in risen-Jesus commissions. Matthew commands an ongoing disciple-making practice; Acts announces an imminent divine act.
edges.label: Baptizing nations and waiting for Spirit baptism

edges.basis: Acts uses John’s baptism both to qualify a witness and to locate the beginning of Jesus’ public story. One passage defines continuous presence; the other gives a theological-historical summary.
edges.label: From John’s baptism to apostolic witness

edges.basis: Both speeches locate John’s baptism at the threshold of Jesus’ public appearance. Peter emphasizes anointing and eyewitness deeds; Paul emphasizes promise, David, repentance, and John’s denial.
edges.label: Peter and Paul place John before Jesus’ ministry

edges.basis: Adjacent Acts scenes preserve people whose knowledge is bounded by John’s baptism. Apollos is privately taught and already speaks accurately; the Ephesian disciples receive baptism and Spirit through Paul’s ministry.
edges.label: Knowing only John’s baptism

edges.basis: Jesus announces Spirit baptism before the ascension, and Peter later identifies its fulfillment pattern in the Gentile Spirit event. The remembered saying connects events without making Jerusalem and Caesarea identical in every detail.
edges.label: The promise and Peter’s remembered application

edges.basis: Both letters connect baptism with burial, raising, and changed life in Christ. Romans develops freedom from sin’s rule; Colossians joins the image to circumcision, debt, and powers.
edges.label: Buried and raised in Romans and Colossians

edges.basis: Galatians and Romans use baptism to speak about belonging and transformed identity. Galatians stresses sonship, unity, and inheritance; Romans stresses death, enslavement, and embodied obedience.
edges.label: Putting on Christ and walking in new life

edges.basis: Peter explicitly names baptism while Titus names washing and renewal by the Spirit. Titus never names baptism, and Peter explicitly denies that bodily washing defines the saving claim.
edges.label: Baptism, washing, and the Spirit

edges.basis: Mark first narrates Jesus’ water baptism and later places baptism language on his coming suffering. The later metaphor shares the word while changing action, setting, agent, and outcome.
edges.label: The Jordan baptism and a baptism of suffering

edges.basis: Mark and Luke preserve Jesus speaking of a baptism still to be received after the Jordan. Mark joins it to cup, service, and ransom; Luke joins it to fire, distress, completion, and division.
edges.label: A cup, a baptism, and coming distress

edges.basis: Matthew repeats beloved-Son and divine-pleasure language in two major scenes. The mountain adds visible disciples, Moses, Elijah, cloud, transformation, and a command to listen.
edges.label: The beloved-Son voice at river and mountain

edges.basis: Matthew narrates the scene and 2 Peter claims remembered hearing of the majestic voice. The later witness uses the shared beloved-Son language while locating it specifically on the holy mountain.
edges.label: The mountain scene and an eyewitness memory

event.centerRule: The Baptism of Jesus remains the Event center. Related texts enter only when they materially prepare, witness, interpret, remember, contrast, or reuse the Event, and every Gospel witness keeps its own wording and sequence.

event.throughline: The trail moves from prophetic language and John’s preparation through four distinct Gospel witnesses, immediate aftermath, later testimony, apostolic memory, and bounded baptismal reuse.

topic.orientation: Enter the baptism through each Gospel witness, then follow the words, actions, testimony, aftermath, and later memory that Scripture places around it.

nodes.note: A shoot from Jesse receives the Spirit of wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, and fear of the LORD.
nodes.title: The Spirit rests on the shoot from Jesse

nodes.note: Comfort is announced, a wilderness voice commands preparation, and the LORD comes with power while tending his flock.
nodes.title: A voice prepares the LORD’s way

nodes.note: God presents a chosen servant, delights in him, and puts his Spirit on him for justice among the nations.
nodes.title: God delights in the servant and puts the Spirit on him

nodes.note: The speaker says the Lord’s Spirit is on him because the LORD has anointed him to announce good news and release.
nodes.title: The Spirit and anointing commission proclamation

nodes.note: The LORD sends a messenger to prepare the way before the desired lord and covenant messenger comes.
nodes.title: A messenger prepares for a sudden arrival

nodes.note: The closing oracle calls Israel to remember Moses and promises Elijah before the great day.
nodes.title: Elijah is promised before the day of the LORD

pivots.title: Voices before the Jordan

pivots.description: John calls Israel to repent, baptizes in water, and points beyond his own work to the coming one.

nodes.note: John appears in Judea’s wilderness, announces the Kingdom, baptizes confessing people, confronts leaders, and speaks of one stronger.
nodes.title: John calls for repentance and points to the coming one

nodes.note: Mark opens with prophetic words, John’s baptism of repentance for forgiveness, and testimony about the stronger one.
nodes.title: Mark joins messenger, wilderness, forgiveness, and promise

nodes.note: The word of God comes to John in a named political and priestly setting; he announces repentance, answers crowds, and denies being the Christ.
nodes.title: Luke dates John’s call and records its social demands

nodes.note: John tells Jerusalem’s delegation that he is not the Christ, Elijah, or the prophet, then identifies himself with Isaiah’s voice.
nodes.title: John denies three identities and names a present unknown one

pivots.title: John prepares the way

pivots.description: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John preserve distinct evidence: arrival, reluctance, prayer, opened heaven, Spirit, voice, sign, testimony, and following.

nodes.note: Jesus comes from Galilee to be baptized; John resists, Jesus answers, and the baptism proceeds.
nodes.title: Jesus comes to John and speaks of fulfilling righteousness

nodes.note: Jesus comes from Nazareth, is baptized by John, and immediately sees the heavens torn open and the Spirit descending.
nodes.title: The heavens are torn open over Jesus

nodes.note: After all the people are baptized, Jesus is baptized and prays; heaven opens.
nodes.title: Jesus prays as heaven opens

nodes.note: John calls Jesus God’s Lamb, says Jesus ranks before him, and explains that the purpose of his water baptism was Israel’s recognition.
nodes.title: John identifies Jesus by a descending and remaining Spirit

nodes.note: John again identifies Jesus as God’s Lamb, two disciples follow, and Andrew brings Simon.
nodes.title: John’s testimony sends disciples after Jesus

pivots.title: The baptism in four witnesses

pivots.description: Each Synoptic witness carries Jesus from baptism into wilderness testing and the beginning of public proclamation.

nodes.note: Immediately after the baptism, the Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness where the tempter repeatedly challenges his sonship.
nodes.title: The Spirit leads the beloved Son into testing

nodes.note: The Spirit immediately drives Jesus into the wilderness for forty days with Satan, wild animals, and angels.
nodes.title: The Spirit drives Jesus into wilderness before proclamation

nodes.note: Jesus returns from the Jordan full of the Holy Spirit and is led in the wilderness through forty days of temptation.
nodes.title: Full of the Spirit, Jesus is led and tested

nodes.note: Jesus returns in the Spirit’s power, reads Isaiah 61, and announces its fulfillment in the listeners’ hearing.
nodes.title: Spirit-anointed proclamation reaches Nazareth

pivots.title: From Jordan into testing and proclamation

pivots.description: Later exchanges preserve John’s testimony, declining prominence, uncertainty, imprisonment, and death.

nodes.note: Jesus’ disciples baptize while John is still baptizing; a purification dispute prompts concern about growing attention to Jesus.
nodes.title: A baptism dispute leads John to speak of increase and decrease

nodes.note: Jesus learns that the Pharisees heard he was making and baptizing more disciples than John.
nodes.title: The disciples’ baptizing becomes publicly noticed

nodes.note: From prison John sends disciples to ask Jesus whether he is the coming one.
nodes.title: John asks whether Jesus is the coming one

nodes.note: John’s disciples report Jesus’ deeds; John sends two to ask whether he is the coming one.
nodes.title: Luke preserves John’s question after Jesus heals

nodes.note: Herod imprisons John because John challenges his marriage; a banquet promise leads to John’s beheading.
nodes.title: John is executed after confronting Herod

nodes.note: Mark reports Herod’s puzzled protection of John, Herodias’ hostility, the banquet, and the forced execution.
nodes.title: Mark expands Herod’s fear and John’s death

pivots.title: John keeps pointing beyond himself

pivots.description: Jesus asks leaders to account for John’s baptism, and later disciples remember the baptism as part of Jesus’ public beginning.

nodes.note: When leaders challenge Jesus’ authority, he asks whether John’s baptism came from heaven or humans.
nodes.title: Jesus asks leaders to judge John’s baptism

nodes.note: Chief priests, scribes, and elders ask by what authority Jesus acts; he answers with a question about John’s baptism.
nodes.title: Mark links Jesus’ authority question to John’s baptism

nodes.note: While Jesus teaches in the Temple, leaders demand the source of his authority; he asks about John’s baptism.
nodes.title: Luke preserves the same authority deadlock

nodes.note: Jesus claims all authority and sends the eleven to make disciples of all nations.
nodes.title: The risen Jesus commissions baptism among all nations

pivots.title: The baptism becomes a public question

pivots.description: Acts repeatedly locates Jesus’ ministry, witness, and the promise of the Spirit in relation to John’s baptism.

nodes.note: The risen Jesus teaches about God’s Kingdom and tells the apostles to wait in Jerusalem for the Father’s promise.
nodes.title: Jesus contrasts John’s water baptism with the Spirit promise

nodes.note: Peter requires a replacement witness who accompanied the group from John’s baptism until Jesus’ ascension.
nodes.title: Apostolic witness is traced from John’s baptism

nodes.note: Peter summarizes the word proclaimed through Judea beginning from Galilee after John’s baptism.
nodes.title: Peter begins Jesus’ public story after John’s baptism

nodes.note: Paul retells Israel’s story through David to the promised Savior, then names John’s baptism of repentance before Jesus’ coming.
nodes.title: Paul places John before Jesus’ coming

nodes.note: Apollos is eloquent, powerful in Scripture, instructed in the Lord’s way, and fervent, yet knows only John’s baptism.
nodes.title: Apollos teaches accurately while knowing only John’s baptism

nodes.note: Paul meets disciples who have not heard about the Holy Spirit and asks into what they were baptized.
nodes.title: Disciples of John receive fuller instruction

nodes.note: Peter explains the Spirit’s coming on Gentiles by remembering the Lord’s contrast between John’s water baptism and baptism in the Holy Spirit.
nodes.title: Peter remembers Jesus’ words about John and the Spirit

pivots.title: The event in apostolic proclamation

pivots.description: Later Scripture reuses baptism, water, Spirit, death, burial, clothing, washing, and appeal language without collapsing those texts into the Jordan event.

nodes.note: Paul asks whether grace permits continued sin and answers by describing baptism into Christ Jesus and into his death.
nodes.title: Baptism is described through death, burial, and new life

nodes.note: Paul contrasts custody under law with faith’s arrival and calls believers God’s children through faith in Christ Jesus.
nodes.title: Baptism is joined to putting on Christ

nodes.note: The letter locates divine fullness in Christ and believers’ fullness in him.
nodes.title: Baptism joins burial, raising, forgiveness, and victory

nodes.note: Christ suffers once, is made alive in the Spirit, and the passage moves through imprisoned spirits, Noah, ark, and flood.
nodes.title: Noah’s water is carried into a baptism statement

nodes.note: The letter recalls former folly and hostility, then says God’s kindness appeared and salvation came by mercy rather than righteous works.
nodes.title: Washing and renewal are attributed to divine mercy

nodes.note: James and John ask for honored seats; Jesus asks whether they can drink his cup or receive his baptism.
nodes.title: Jesus names a cup and baptism of suffering

nodes.note: Jesus speaks of casting fire on the earth and of a baptism he must undergo, saying he is distressed until it is completed.
nodes.title: Jesus speaks of a baptism still ahead

pivots.title: Baptism language after the event

pivots.description: The transfiguration and its later memory repeat beloved-Son language in a new setting and preserve a distinct eyewitness claim.

nodes.note: Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James, and John; Moses and Elijah appear, and a bright cloud overshadows them.
nodes.title: The beloved-Son voice is heard on the mountain

nodes.note: Peter denies following myths and describes being an eyewitness of Jesus’ majesty.
nodes.title: Peter remembers hearing the majestic voice
